# Code review {#code-review}

::: {.tada-key}
**Code review** is the process of either **formally** (as part of the
peer-review process) or **informally** (as co-authors or colleagues) checking
and evaluating each other's code. It is critical to help avoid **conceptual,
programmatic, and syntactic errors**, and it can take place at any stage of the
research cycle.
:::

This chapter follows Ivimey-Cook et al. (2023), *Implementing code review in
the scientific workflow: Insights from ecology and evolutionary biology*
(Journal of Evolutionary Biology 36: 1347–1356,
<https://doi.org/10.1111/jeb.14230>).

## Why it is missing, and why it matters {#review-why}

Researchers increasingly rely on code written in open-source software such as R
and Python to clean, manipulate, visualise and analyse data. Code-based
software is more transparent and reproducible than point-and-click software,
and far more flexible — researchers can tailor analyses to their exact needs.

But that flexibility comes at a cost: **code is more error-prone**, and several
high-profile retractions have centred on exactly this kind of mistake.

In computer science and software development, code review is routine. In the
academic disciplines that rely on code to make inferences and predictions, it
is **noticeably absent** from the research and publication process. The paper
argues for a fundamental shift in research culture that brings code review into
**all stages** of the research process.

There is a structural reason it does not happen. Informal training, combined
with insufficient time and incentives, means that coding and analysis are
usually the responsibility of **a single member of a team** for a project's
entire lifetime — in stark contrast to the team-wide collaboration that is
normal when developing methodology and experimental design. That individual
nature of research code is precisely what makes pre-publication code review
both unlikely and critical.

## The four Rs {#review-four-rs}

Whatever the stage, the core priorities are the same. The paper frames them as
four questions.

::: {.tada-cards}
::: {.tada-card .t}
[R]{.tada-letter} [Reported]{.tada-word}
[Does the code match the description of what is reported in the methods
section?]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .a1}
[R]{.tada-letter} [Run]{.tada-word}
[Can the code actually be executed?]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .d}
[R]{.tada-letter} [Reliable]{.tada-word}
[Does it do the right thing — not just *something* — every time?]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .a2}
[R]{.tada-letter} [Reproducible]{.tada-word}
[Do the outputs match the results reported in the paper?]{.tada-gloss}
:::
:::

::: {.tabset}

### Reported {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Code is a key research output and a critical component of scientific
methodology. Open code accompanying written methods sections is becoming more
common, following the same push that produced Open and FAIR data. So the first
check is **consistency between the code and the manuscript**. These questions
catch **conceptual** errors.

*Does the code match what the methods section says was done?* If the methods
state a generalised linear model with Poisson error, and the code fits a
Gaussian one, that mismatch has to be part of the review.

**Software and package versions.** At minimum, the packages that are integral
to the analysis or to visualisation should be listed, with version numbers,
somewhere in the manuscript. In R these can be obtained with `citation()`; in
Python, using `setuptools`. A full list of everything used — including packages
involved in cleaning and tidying — can go elsewhere, such as an associated `.R`
or `.py` file.

This matters beyond bookkeeping: it means that if a package version is later
found to contain a bug, papers depending on it can be identified.

**Environment management** helps here. Packages such as **`renv`**
(Ushey & Wickham 2023, which replaces `packrat`) and **`groundhog`**
(Simonsohn & Gruson 2023) in R, or **`poetry`** (Eustace 2023) and **`pipenv`**
(Pipenv Maintainer Team 2023) in Python, help ensure a reproducible
environment and allow specific package versions to be loaded. Containerisation
with **Docker** is another option.

### Run {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Even if code matches the methodology reported in a paper, that does not mean it
is executable. **Programmatic and syntactic errors** can make code fail to
re-run.

Common causes:

- calls to libraries or modules that are not installed in the current
  environment
- local or absolute file paths that do not exist on the reviewer's machine
- missing files, or filenames in the code that do not match the archived files
- a missing code chunk

This is the cheapest check to perform and the one that fails most often — recall
that **74% of over 9,000 archived R files** failed to complete without error.

::: {.tada-tip}
Run it in a **fresh session**, from a **fresh download**, in a **new folder**.
Anything that only works because of what is already loaded in your environment
will fail here, which is the point.
:::

### Reliable {.unlisted .unnumbered}

The hardest of the four, and the one that most needs a human who knows the
study.

Errors can propagate through code that runs perfectly well and produces an
output, because **code can produce incorrect results in a reproducible manner**
— the same wrong answer, every time. The paper's example: if code selects or
modifies the wrong column in a dataset, the analysis is wrong but nothing
errors.

**Unit testing** helps: **`testthat`** (Wickham 2011) in R, **`pytest`**
(Okken 2022) in Python. But this type of error remains common and is
**extremely difficult to pick up by anyone without deep familiarity with the
dataset and code**. It is also thought to scale with the number of lines and
the complexity of the code.

::: {.tada-note}
This is the strongest argument for **co-author** review over external review. A
reviewer who does not know your data cannot tell that `mass` should have been
`mass_g`. A co-author can.
:::

### Reproducible {.unlisted .unnumbered}

The most fundamental question: **can the code produce the output, and thus
support the conclusions, given in the paper?**

The final step of code review is ensuring that outputs, when the code is
re-run, match those reported in the analysis and results sections — including
relevant figures and the narrative text within those sections.

**When exact matching is not possible.** Some tolerance must be applied,
especially with stochastic methods where parameter estimates change between
runs, or with techniques that are computationally demanding and slow. This
happens, for example, when `set.seed()` (R) or `random.seed()` (Python) was not
used before stochastic sampling.

Providing model outputs helps — save them with `saveRDS()` in R or
`pickle.dump()` in Python — though it does not let a reviewer run the code
themselves to see whether they obtain similar results. Where the code cannot be
re-run in reasonable time, newly generated results should be compared against
the originally reported ones.

**Two ways to judge a match:**

*Conclusion and numbers* (Archmiller et al. 2020). Compare the **conclusion**
(direction and significance level) and the **numbers** (intervals matching
within one significant figure). Their worked example:

| Original | Reproduced | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| mean 4.00, interval 3.30–5.00 | mean 4.12, interval 3.45–4.91 | Conclusion **and** numbers reproduced |
| mean 4.00, interval 3.30–5.00 | mean 6.5, interval 6.0–7.0 | Same conclusion; numbers **not** quantitatively reproduced |
| mean 4.00, interval 3.30–5.00 | mean 4.10, interval −1.00–8.40 | **Not** reproduced — the interval now overlaps zero |

*Percentage error* (Hardwicke et al. 2021; see also Kambouris et al. 2023).
Comparison at one significant figure is highly dependent on scale; percentage
error is not. Using

$$\text{PE} = \frac{\text{new} - \text{original}}{\text{original}} \times 100$$

error is classified as **non-existent** when this value is 0, **minor** between
0 and 10, and **major (and not reproducible)** at 10 or above.

Importantly: as well as the overlap with 0 (or the null hypothesis) not
changing, the reported and reproduced estimates and intervals should not
significantly differ from each other. With stochastic MCMC methods, variation
between chains is expected to be much lower than variation within a chain, so
the reproduced value should sit well within the reported credible interval.

:::

## Writing reviewable code {#review-reviewable}

Good readability is what makes effective code review possible at all. Four
quick solutions from the paper:

1. **Call packages explicitly** via the namespace — `package::function()` in R,
   `package.module.function()` in Python.
2. **Use relative file paths** — e.g. the `here` package (Müller 2020),
   preferably with an associated R project file if using R and RStudio, or a
   virtual environment in Python.
3. **Remove redundant packages.**
4. **Write analysis code with clear subheadings, intuitive comments and
   easy-to-understand object names.**

**Formatters** apply a standard style in one command: **`styler`**
(Müller & Walthert 2020) in R, **`pycodestyle`** (Rocholl 2022) in Python.
Both support standardised styles — Google, tidyverse in R, PEP 8 in Python.

**Literate formats** — R/Python Markdown, Quarto, or Jupyter Notebook /
JupyterLab — present code in chunks which, with suitably descriptive comments,
are far easier to read. See [Annotated](#annotated-literate).

### Structure {.unlisted .unnumbered}

A simple folder and file structure goes a long way towards helping researchers
at all skill levels understand the **order and flow** of an analysis:

- **Sequentially labelled** subfolders and scripts, so someone following the
  code knows the order to run things in — files beginning `01…`, `02…`
- **Folders named for their purpose** — `data`, `scripts`, `functions`
- **Raw data kept separate**, so it is not accidentally modified or overwritten
  when cleaning or wrangling code runs
- A **README** and additional metadata giving the signposts needed to re-run
  the code: packages and version numbers, descriptions of the data files, the
  project aim, author contact details, and any licences in place

It is also crucial to **explain what data cleaning or curation happened before
the analysis code** — what previous manipulation or pre-processing produced the
data in its current state, or where an intermediate data file was used.

::: {.tada-note}
**Metadata tooling.** Packages such as `codemeta` (Boettiger 2017) and
`dataReporter` (Petersen & Ekstrøm 2019) in R, or `CodeMetaPy` (van Gompel 2023)
and `cookiecutter` (Feldroy 2022) in Python, can help produce consistent
metadata and project templates. **Pipeline tools** — `targets` (Landau 2021),
`workflowr` (Blischak et al. 2019) in R, or `luigi` in Python — automate the
steps from raw dataset to results.
:::

## When code review happens {#review-when}

Code review can begin as early as the first initiation of a project, and has a
role beyond publication.

::: {.tabset}

### Pre-submission {.unlisted .unnumbered}

**This is where most of the value is.** It is also the stage where a reviewer
can catch *Reliable* errors, because they know the study.

Keep **continuous code collaboration at all stages** of a manuscript.
Collaboration can be facilitated by code-sharing platforms such as GitHub,
where users can submit and comment on pull requests. At SORTEE, GitHub issues
were used to summarise the discussion of an individual's code.

The [SORTEE guidelines](#sortee) recommend the same thing from the journal
side: send the project to a colleague or co-author before submission. They can
check that the code runs with the data in the structure provided, that the
metadata is adequate, that data and code match the manuscript, and that the
results reproduce. And co-authors are more likely to spot mistakes in the code
than an outsider, because they know the study and the data.

### During peer review {.unlisted .unnumbered}

One of the most crucial places for code review, because reviewers can carefully
follow the logic of the analyses much as they follow the argument from
introduction to discussion.

Some journals already request code and data at submission — The Royal Society;
*Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology*. In some cases, such as the **Journal of
Open Source Software**, the entire formal peer-review process, code and
manuscript alike, is hosted on GitHub.

The benefits run both ways: for authors, providing code during peer review
could increase manuscript quality; for reviewers, available code gives far
deeper insight, because there is a clearer link between experimental
methodology and statistical analysis — the first R, code **as reported**.

**The hurdles are real, though.**

*Finding reviewers.* There is already a shortage of willing reviewers. It is
reasonable to expect a reviewer to check that code is **as reported**; anything
deeper takes time from already overworked academics who may not have the exact
expertise. A workable compromise: reviewers state whether they are competent to
check that the code is as reported, and the journal ensures **at least one**
reviewer has checked the code.

*Double-blind review.* Anonymised data and code can be submitted directly to
the journal (e.g. as a zip file), or uploaded to figshare, OSF, GitHub or Dryad,
which allow authors to provide an **anonymised link** for peer review.

### Post-publication {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Much less discussed. It does not prevent publication of incorrect results, but
it does allow checking whether the code adheres to the four Rs.

The first question is simply: **has all the code used to produce the results
been made available?** If not, the main option is to contact the corresponding
author — or the journal — and ask, much as data is requested "upon reasonable
request".

**If you find that the code does not adhere to one of the Rs:**

1. **Contact the corresponding author** — or, if the paper uses the MeRIT
   system, the person who actually conducted the analysis. A GitHub issue works
   well if there is a repository; otherwise, email.
2. **Rule out benign causes** first: differences in software version (R or
   package versions), or inherent stochasticity (simulations, MCMC sampling).
3. **Let the authors go to the journal themselves.** If there is a genuine
   error, authors should be given the chance to contact the journal to
   highlight and correct their own mistake.

::: {.tada-note}
Journal culture matters here. Under *The American Naturalist*'s stance, authors
who contact the journal to correct code or data errors are **not penalised**,
and corrections are encouraged where warranted. Where updated results would
alter the narrative of a published paper, corrections are harder; publication
versioning or "living" documents may be a first step.
:::

:::

## Running a code club {#review-club}

One of the most effective ways to establish a culture of peer code review in a
lab or among colleagues. The following draws on the authors' experience
building a code review club in collaboration with **SORTEE**.

The barriers being addressed are worth naming, because the design of the club
follows from them: **lack of time and incentive**, **lack of technical
knowledge and unclear workflows**, and **social pressures and the fear of being
judged by peers**.

### Set a clear goal for each session {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Is the focus **general learning and improving readability**, or is it to
**error-check and scrutinise reproducibility**? Having a clear structure and
goal for each session focuses comments and advice on the precise reason for the
review.

Related: unless the aim is specifically to evaluate different analytical
options, it is better to **leave methodological questions aside**. A code
review that drifts into "have you considered a different model?" stops being a
code review.

### Make it a judgement-free environment {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Volunteers often feel very anxious about showing code that may have errors. It
is vital to **normalise the existence of errors** and to highlight that
perfection is never possible. It is also useful to stress that **there is no
such thing as bad code**, and that there are usually multiple ways to approach
the same problem.

### Think about group size {.unlisted .unnumbered}

A **smaller group** is a friendlier starting point: people feel more
comfortable speaking up, and it better facilitates peer-to-peer learning and
focused review.

**Larger groups** work better for wider discussion of general themes and tips.

Decide by aim: general discussion → bigger; focused review of code → smaller.

### Decide on credit {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Code review outside the formal peer-review process can have a large impact on a
project, from error checking to validating that statistical analyses are
appropriate. So what should reviewers get?

- **Acknowledgement via MeRIT** (Method Reporting with Initials for
  Transparency) — for example: *"…mixed model with a Gaussian error
  distribution. Code was checked by E.I.C."*
- **Co-authorship**, where the review fundamentally altered the project and the
  resulting paper — for instance, where a reviewer finds a major coding error
  that, once fixed, changes the results and conclusions.

The principle: **incentives should be relative to the impact of the reviewer on
the project.**

## A reviewer's script {#review-script}

Wiki guidance — a practical sequence for a single review session, built on the
four Rs. The full checklist is at
[`templates/code-review-checklist.md`](templates/code-review-checklist.md).

**Before the session (reviewer, 20 minutes)**

1. Download the project into a **new, empty folder**.
2. Open the README. Can you tell what to run, in what order, and what you need
   installed? Note anything you had to guess.
3. Try to run it, in a **fresh session**. Record every error verbatim, and stop
   at the first one you cannot resolve in two minutes.

**In the session**

4. **Reported** — walk the methods section against the code, section by
   section. Flag anything described in the paper you cannot find in the code,
   and anything in the code not described in the paper.
5. **Run** — go through the errors you hit. Most will be environment or path
   problems, and most are quick.
6. **Reliable** — pick the two or three steps where a silent error would matter
   most (the filtering step, the join, the model specification) and read them
   closely with the author. Ask what each column is.
7. **Reproducible** — take three numbers from the results section and find them
   in the output.

**Afterwards**

8. Write it up as a short list, ordered by severity, separating **must fix**
   from **would be nice**.
9. Agree how the reviewer will be credited.

::: {.tada-tip}
**Give feedback on the code, not the coder.** "This line reads `mass` — is that
the right column?" lands very differently from "you used the wrong column".
Given that fear of judgement is one of the three named barriers to code review,
this is not just politeness; it is what keeps people volunteering.
:::

## Checklist {#review-checklist}

- [ ] **Reported** — the code does what the methods section says it does
- [ ] Software and key packages, with versions, are stated
- [ ] **Run** — the code executes from a fresh download in a fresh session
- [ ] All required libraries are installed and loaded within the code
- [ ] File paths are relative and resolve
- [ ] **Reliable** — filtering, joins and model specifications have been read closely by someone who knows the data
- [ ] Seeds are set before stochastic steps
- [ ] **Reproducible** — spot-checked numbers from the results section match the output
- [ ] Mismatches are explained (version, stochasticity, post-processing) and documented
- [ ] Slow or proprietary steps have saved outputs archived
- [ ] The reviewer's contribution is credited (MeRIT, acknowledgement, or authorship)
